articleSummary:
- DR Congo's Ebola outbreak has surpassed 4,000 confirmed cases, reaching 4,053 with 1,850 deaths as of 9 August 2026. Declared May 15, it is the second-largest Ebola epidemic on record and the fastest-spreading, behind only the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak (Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone, ~28,000). True scale likely higher; analyses suggest the virus was active in Ituri by January or earlier, with more than 500 suspected cases from mid-Jan to May 15. Confirmed infections are in five provinces: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo. Delayed detection, overstretched surveillance, ongoing conflict, and lack of approved vaccines or treatments for this strain have allowed the disease to outrun containment, with displacement and insecurity further complicating response.
- Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ituri province continues since mid-May, with the region bearing the heaviest burden. Official figures show over 300 child deaths, accounting for roughly one-quarter of infections but nearly one-third of fatalities. More than 1 million people are displaced by conflict, with women and children making up about 80% of the displaced. UNICEF reports maternal mortality in Ituri has nearly doubled since the outbreak began, averaging six pregnancy-related deaths per week; pregnant women with Ebola face high miscarriage risk. On August 5–6, 2026, Endemic Control Agents Adriane Schmitz, Fabiane Amaral, Laudecir Kirsten, and Elias Morais attended a Technical Training organized by the 2nd Regional Health Coordination (2ª CRS) in partnership with the State Center for Health Surveillance (CEVS), the Frederico Westphalen Municipal Health Department, and Agrocontinental. The training, held at the Frederico Westphalen Exposition Park, covered theoretical and practical use of equipment for arbovirus field actions, including motorized ULV equipment, the BRi battery, and heavy ULV gear, with hands-on sessions to improve application, maintenance, and operation. This initiative supports ongoing capacity building to enhance dengue and other arboviral disease prevention and control in the municipality, protecting public health.

articleSummary: Rio Branco is among Brazilian capitals—Manaus, Porto Alegre, Curitiba, Florianópolis, Belo Horizonte, Salvador and São Luís—in alert/at-risk/high-risk SRAG activity per the Fiocruz InfoGripe bulletin (Aug 6, 2026). SRAG burden is higher in young children, while influenza A is a major mortality driver among older adults. Recommendations: up-to-date vaccination, regular handwashing, avoiding close contact with symptomatic individuals, and masking in health facilities; symptomatic people should stay home or wear a mask when leaving the house.

articleHeadline: Leishmaniasis, known as kala-azar, continues to pose a challenge to public health; learn how to identify the warning signs.
articleSummary: Visceral leishmaniasis, known as kala-azar, is a zoonotic disease that remains a challenge for veterinary and public health. WHO notes Brazil is among six countries that account for about 90% of cases. The Agosto Verde campaign aims to raise awareness on prevention, early diagnosis, and control, focusing on endemic regions—North, Northeast, interior of São Paulo, and Mato Grosso do Sul—where urban expansion has increased contact with the vector. Transmission occurs by sandfly bite, with dogs as the main reservoir; human-to-dog or dog-to-human transmission is not direct. Symptoms in dogs include dermatologic signs (alopecia, crusting around eyes and ears, non-healing wounds, nose depigmentation), plus weight loss, apathy, lameness, epistaxis, and ocular issues. Diagnosis starts with serologic blood tests and a screening test, followed by confirmatory laboratory or molecular tests on skin, bone marrow, or lymph nodes. Early detection reduces spread and organ damage; mortality often stems from chronic kidney disease.

articleHeadline: Seasonal flu can cause serious complications even in healthy children.
articleSummary: Seasonal influenza can cause serious complications in children in Vietnam. At Bach Mai Hospital, Dr. Pham Cong Khac notes flu is a viral respiratory illness; most children recover in a week with proper care, but severe outcomes occur even in healthy kids. Symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, nasal congestion, and myalgia; younger children may be irritable, poorly fed, vomiting, or lethargic. Complications range from dehydration and asthma exacerbation to pneumonia, respiratory failure, myocarditis, encephalitis, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, shock, and multi-organ failure requiring ICU. High-risk groups include under-5s, under 2; congenital heart disease, chronic lung or neurological conditions, diabetes, immune suppression, and cancer. A 2026 US Pediatrics study found vaccinated children had about 80% lower influenza mortality (2016–2025). US guidelines advise annual vaccination for all 6 months+. Inactivated vaccines cannot cause flu; mild reactions are common. Prevention includes vaccination, hand hygiene, covering coughs, masking when needed, and keeping feverish children home.

articleSummary: Thailand reports 557,993 cumulative HIV cases, with new infections down about 12,000 over the past three years. articleHeadline: Kim Kardashian, bikini-clad on a lake paddle boat... "This creature" that invades through the nose—watch out?
articleSummary: Naegleria fowleri (brain-eating amoeba) poses a fatal risk in warm freshwater lakes, rivers, and ponds, especially during summer, when water exposure occurs via the nose rather than ingestion. In the United States, primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) cases are typically under 10 per year and are almost always fatal. Korea reported its first domestically confirmed death from N. fowleri in December 2022—a 50-year-old man who had spent about four months in Thailand before returning. A 2017 Korean study detected N. fowleri in 6 of 52 raw-water samples (11.5%), indicating domestic presence. Prevention includes keeping the nose closed (nose clips) or pinching the nose while diving, avoiding stirring lake sediments, and staying out of warm water when the nose would be exposed. Shoreline risk also includes ticks and snakes; wear long clothing, use repellents, perform thorough checks after outdoor activity, and seek prompt care if bitten. Sun exposure and heat illness (heat exhaustion/heat stroke) are additional concerns; reapply broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen every 2 hours.

articleHeadline: Service Above Self: Will malaria return to N. America?
articleSummary: Malaria remains a global threat as the United States completed its withdrawal from WHO on Jan 22, 2026, cutting 18% of the agency’s resources and limiting access to international data. About 282 million people are infected annually, with 610,000 deaths, 75% of them under five. In Canada, roughly 488 imported malaria cases are recorded each year, mostly among travelers from endemic areas. Rotarians Against Malaria, a Rotary Global Action Group, has expanded elimination efforts, with Rotary Foundation funding the first Program of Scale in Zambia. WHO has approved two vaccines against liver-stage parasites; PlasProtecT, supported by Rotary partners in Australia and nearing clinical trials, can be freeze-dried for transport and targets parasites after they leave the liver. Ongoing challenges include insecticide resistance, funding cuts, conflicts, trade disruptions, displacement, vaccine resistance, and data-sharing limits, heightening risk to Canada and North America amid imported cases.
